title: uv

[uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) is a package and project manager for Python.
It installs Python itself and the packages a project needs from
[PyPI](https://pypi.org) into an environment that belongs to the project, and
it records the exact versions that were installed, such that a collaborator, a
cluster or a CI run gets the same environment as you have locally. It replaces
`pip`, `venv` and tools such as Poetry, and it is very fast.

{{< include _uv-or-pixi.qmd >}}

## Installation

On macOS and Linux, run the following in a terminal:

```bash
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
```

On Windows, run the following in PowerShell:

```powershell
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"
```

Restart the terminal afterwards and check that the installation worked with

```bash
uv --version
```

Other ways of installing, e.g. with Homebrew, are described in the
[official installation guide](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/).
When uv was installed with the installer above, it updates itself with
`uv self update`.

## Writing a script

A script, or a few related scripts, is kept in a folder of its own together
with its environment. The folder is set up with

```bash
mkdir spectra-analysis
cd spectra-analysis
uv init --bare
```

which writes a minimal `pyproject.toml` and nothing else. Without `--bare`,
`uv init` sets the folder up as a package, which is described
[below](#writing-a-package) and is more than a script needs.

::: {.callout-note}
The group's [`/python:script`](../ai/skills.qmd#skill-python-script) skill for
Claude Code sets up and writes scripts in this way, and explains how to run
them afterwards.
:::

### Choosing the Python version

uv downloads and installs the Python version a project needs, so it does not
matter which Python, if any, is installed on the system. The version is chosen
when the project is created,

```bash
uv init --bare --python 3.12
```

which sets `requires-python = ">=3.12"` in `pyproject.toml`. To fix the exact
version used in the folder, run

```bash
uv python pin 3.12
```

which writes it to a `.python-version` file. `uv python list` shows the
versions that are installed and available.

### Adding packages

A package is added to the project with

```bash
uv add numpy matplotlib
```

which records it in `pyproject.toml`, installs it into the environment in
`.venv/` and updates the lock file `uv.lock`. A requirement on the version is
given in the same way as for pip, e.g. `uv add "numpy>=2"`, and a package is
removed again with `uv remove`.

### Running

The script is run with

```bash
uv run analyse.py
```

`uv run` first checks that the environment in `.venv/` matches `pyproject.toml`
and `uv.lock`, installs or updates packages if it does not, and then runs the
script with the Python of that environment. There is nothing to activate, and
a colleague who runs the same command gets the same packages. Any other command
is run in the environment in the same way, e.g. `uv run python` for an
interactive session.

Alternatively, the environment can be activated as an ordinary virtual
environment,

```bash
source .venv/bin/activate
python analyse.py
```

on Windows with `.venv\Scripts\activate`, and `deactivate` leaves it again.
This is a perfectly reasonable way of working, but it takes a little more
care: `python` then runs whatever is installed in `.venv/` at the time, so
after changing `pyproject.toml` or pulling changes from a collaborator, run
`uv sync` to bring the environment up to date. Without an activated
environment, `python analyse.py` uses whichever Python comes first on the
system rather than the project's. Packages should still be added with
`uv add` rather than `pip install`, such that they are recorded in
`pyproject.toml`.

Editors such as VS Code find the environment in `.venv/` on their own.

### A script in a single file

When a script must travel on its own, e.g. by email, the list of packages can
be written into the script itself instead of a `pyproject.toml`:

```bash
uv init --script analyse.py --python 3.12
uv add --script analyse.py numpy
```

This adds a comment block at the top of the script, and `uv run analyse.py`
reads it and runs the script in an environment with those packages. The
drawback is that editors do not find that environment, so they mark the
imports as missing even though the script runs.

## Writing a package

A Python package, i.e. code that is installed and imported from other scripts
or packages, is created with

```bash
uv init --lib mypackage
```

which creates the following layout:

```
mypackage/
├── .python-version
├── README.md
├── pyproject.toml
└── src/
    └── mypackage/
        ├── __init__.py
        └── py.typed
```

The code of the package goes in `src/mypackage/`, split into modules as it
grows. `pyproject.toml` also contains a `[build-system]` section, which tells
uv how to build and install the package.

### The `src/` layout

The package is placed in a `src/` folder rather than directly in the project
root. If it were in the root, `import mypackage` from the root would import
the folder directly, regardless of whether the package is installed and of
how. With `src/`, the package can only be imported once it is installed, such
that tests and scripts use the package in the same way as anyone else who
installs it, and a missing file or dependency shows up locally rather than for
the next person.

uv installs the package into the project's environment in *editable* mode, so
changes to the code take effect without reinstalling:

```bash
uv run python -c "import mypackage"
```

### Dependency groups

Packages that are needed to work on the package, but not to use it, go in
dependency groups. The `dev` group is installed by default:

```bash
uv add --dev pytest ruff
uv run pytest
```

Further groups, e.g. for building documentation, are added with `--group`:

```bash
uv add --group docs sphinx
uv sync --group docs
```

`uv sync` brings the environment up to date with `pyproject.toml`, and
`--group` or `--all-groups` includes groups other than `dev`. Groups are part
of a single environment, which in most cases is all a package needs. Projects
that need environments that are kept independent of each other are better
served by [Pixi](pixi.qmd#environments).

Dependency groups are not part of the package when it is installed by someone
else. Optional features for the users of a package are instead declared as
*extras*, e.g. `uv add --optional plot matplotlib`, which users install with
`pip install "mypackage[plot]"`.

A package is built into files that can be distributed with `uv build`, and
`uv publish` uploads them to PyPI.

## `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock`

The two files record different things:

`pyproject.toml`
:   The requirements. It lists the packages the project needs, normally with a
    lower bound on the version such as `numpy>=2`, and the Python versions it
    supports. It is the file that you edit, either by hand or with `uv add` and
    `uv remove`.

`uv.lock`
:   The resolution. uv writes it and it records the exact version of every
    package that was installed, including the packages that those depend on in
    turn, for all operating systems at once. It should not be edited by hand.

`.python-version`
:   The Python version used in the folder, if one is pinned.

`.venv/`
:   The environment itself. It can be deleted at any time and is recreated
    from the files above.

`pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock` and `.python-version` should be committed to git,
`.venv/` should not. uv places a `.gitignore` inside `.venv/`, such that git
ignores it without further setup.

For a script, or a project that produces results, the lock file is what makes
the environment reproducible. For a package, the lock file only applies to
working on the package itself: someone who installs it from PyPI or with pip
gets whichever versions satisfy `pyproject.toml` at that time. Its requirements
should therefore describe what the package actually works with, rather than
pinning exact versions.

uv keeps the lock file as it is unless `pyproject.toml` changes. The packages
are updated to the newest versions allowed with

```bash
uv lock --upgrade                 # all packages
uv lock --upgrade-package numpy   # a single package
```

On a CI run, `uv sync --locked` fails if `uv.lock` does not match
`pyproject.toml`, which catches a lock file that was not committed after a
change.

## Tools that are not tied to a project

A command line tool that is distributed as a Python package can be run without
adding it to any project with `uvx`, e.g.

```bash
uvx ruff format analyse.py
```

which installs it into a temporary environment that is cached for later runs.
A tool that is used often is installed permanently with

```bash
uv tool install ruff
```

which makes the `ruff` command available everywhere, in an environment of its
own. `uv tool upgrade --all` updates the installed tools.

## Further reading

The [uv documentation](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) covers all of the above in
more detail, and `uv help` lists the available commands.
